title: Magnetic fields: the Biot-Savart law
voiceInstructions: Warm, engaging female teacher with a natural General American English accent. Relaxed, welcoming and lightly playful, with a gentle smile and conversational rhythm. Keep scientific terms precise and avoid an announcer cadence. Slow down for equations, numbers and conversions. Give brief natural thinking pauses after questions. Do not add words or laughter absent from the script.

sources.title: NTA: Official JEE Main 2026 syllabus, Physics Unit 13
OpenStax: Magnetic field of a current loop

chapters.title: Current creates a magnetic field
chapters.formula: B in tesla; right-hand grip rule uses conventional current; dot = out of page, cross = into page
points: A steady current creates a magnetic field around a wire.
Point your right thumb along conventional current; curled fingers show field direction.
Field direction is distinct from force direction on a test charge.
chapters.script: Hey, welcome back. We've followed charge through electric circuits. Now we ask what a current does to the space around it. A steady current creates a magnetic field, represented by the vector B. Its SI unit is the tesla. A straight wire produces field lines that circle the wire, not lines that point along it. Use your right hand: point your thumb along conventional current, and your curled fingers give the magnetic field direction. Conventional current is opposite electron drift in a metal, so use the current arrow printed in the question. Imagine a vertical wire carrying current upward on the page. To its right, the magnetic field points into the page. To its left, it points out. We represent a vector coming toward you by a dot, like an arrow tip, and one going away by a cross, like the tail of an arrow. Reverse the current and the field reverses. These symbols describe a direction perpendicular to the page; they do not mean a positive or negative field magnitude. Also, do not confuse the direction of magnetic field with the direction of magnetic force on a moving charge. The force requires another vector rule that we will study separately. Our first job is to find B at a chosen observation point. We will use steady currents and thin-wire models in vacuum or approximately air, and state the geometry before applying a formula.

chapters.title: Biot-Savart: add contributions from the wire
chapters.formula: dB = (mu0/4pi) I dl sin(theta)/r^2; vector direction: dl cross r_hat; integrate over the wire
points: r runs from the source current element to the observation point.
theta is the angle between the current element and that displacement.
A single element contribution is not the field of an entire circuit.
chapters.script: The Biot-Savart law connects a small piece of current-carrying wire to its contribution at an observation point. Draw a tiny directed length, d l, along conventional current. Draw the displacement from that piece to the observation point; its magnitude is r. The small field magnitude is mu zero over four pi, multiplied by current, directed-length magnitude and sine theta, then divided by r squared. Theta is the angle between the current element and that displacement. The direction follows d l crossed with the unit displacement vector, using the right-hand cross-product rule. A perpendicular displacement gives the largest contribution for the same current, length and distance. Along the element's direction, sine theta is zero. To obtain the field of a whole wire, add the vector contributions by integration; don't substitute the total wire length into a small-element expression when distance or angle changes. For an approximate tiny segment example, use four amperes, length one centimeter, perpendicular distance ten centimeters. Treat distance and angle as nearly constant across that short piece. With mu zero over four pi approximately ten to the minus seven, its contribution is four times ten to the minus seven tesla, or zero point four microtesla. That is the contribution of this piece, not a complete wire or its return path. In standard JEE numericals we use mu zero approximately four pi times ten to the minus seven tesla meter per ampere. Geometry and vector direction must accompany the arithmetic.

chapters.title: Straight wires: distance and end effects
chapters.formula: Long wire: B = mu0 I/(2pi a); finite segment: B = mu0 I(sin alpha + sin beta)/(4pi a)
points: a is the perpendicular distance from the point to the straight wire.
For the stated finite-segment formula, the perpendicular foot lies between the endpoints.
alpha and beta are measured from the perpendicular toward the endpoints.
chapters.script: For a straight wire, integration gives a useful result. At perpendicular distance a from a wire that is effectively very long in both directions, the field magnitude is mu zero I divided by two pi a. Field strength falls as one over distance, even though a single small-element contribution contains one over r squared. Integration changes the dependence. A five ampere long wire produces twenty microtesla at five centimeters. Double the distance and the field becomes ten microtesla. Now keep the wire finite. If the perpendicular from the observation point meets the segment between its endpoints, define alpha and beta as the positive angles from that perpendicular toward the two endpoint lines. The field is mu zero I divided by four pi a, multiplied by sine alpha plus sine beta. A symmetric segment with both angles forty five degrees, at the same five centimeters and five amperes, gives ten times square root two microtesla, about fourteen point one four. This is smaller than the infinite-wire result because there is less contributing wire. Let both angles approach ninety degrees and the long-wire result returns. If the perpendicular foot lies outside the segment, use signed endpoint geometry or rederive the integral rather than adding two positive sines blindly. The formula gives magnitude; use the current direction to determine into or out of the page. Nearby return wires can also contribute, so read the complete circuit geometry.

chapters.title: Circular loops: symmetry gives an axial field
chapters.formula: Center: B0 = mu0 NI/(2R); axis: B(x) = mu0 NI R^2/[2(R^2+x^2)^(3/2)]
points: At the center, all element contributions share the same perpendicular direction.
On the axis, transverse components cancel while axial components add.
N closely wound identical turns approximately multiply the single-loop field.
chapters.script: A circular loop has a different symmetry. At its center, every current element is perpendicular to the displacement toward the center, and each is the same distance R away. All field contributions point along the loop axis. Integrating around the circumference gives mu zero I divided by two R. For N closely wound identical turns carrying the same current, multiply by N, provided their radii and positions are approximately the same. Curl your right fingers along the loop current; your thumb gives the central field direction. Counterclockwise current as viewed on the page gives field out of the page at the center. For a single loop of radius ten centimeters carrying four amperes, the center field is eight pi microtesla, approximately twenty five point one three. Along the axis at distance x from the center, contributions have transverse components that cancel in opposite pairs. Their axial components add. The result is mu zero N I R squared divided by twice the quantity R squared plus x squared raised to three halves. Set x equal to zero and the center formula returns. Set x equal to R and the field is the center value divided by two square root two, here about eight point eight nine microtesla. This equation is for points on the axis, not arbitrary points in the plane of the loop. State whether a question asks for the center, an axial point or another geometry before choosing the expression.

chapters.title: Arcs and superposition: include direction
chapters.formula: Arc center: B = mu0 I theta/(4pi R), theta in radians; net B is a vector sum
points: A semicircular arc contributes half the complete-loop center field.
Radial straight leads give zero contribution at the center; other lead geometry may not.
Add signed collinear fields or vector components, not unsigned magnitudes automatically.
chapters.script: Let's finish with two common JEE patterns. For a circular arc, the center-field contribution is proportional to the angle swept out. The magnitude is mu zero I times theta divided by four pi R, with theta in radians. A semicircle has theta equal to pi, so its contribution is half that of a full loop with the same radius and current. Our four ampere, ten centimeter semicircular arc contributes four pi microtesla, about twelve point five seven. Its direction still follows the current around the arc. Straight leads directed radially toward or away from that center contribute zero there, because their current elements and displacement vectors are parallel. This is a geometry statement, not a rule that all connecting leads have zero field. Include other lead contributions when needed. Now place two very long parallel wires ten centimeters apart, each carrying five amperes upward. At the midpoint, each gives twenty microtesla, but one field enters the page and the other leaves, so they cancel. Reverse the current in one wire and both midpoint fields point the same way, giving forty microtesla. Notice that these are field comparisons, not statements about forces between the wires. For your final checklist, identify the observation point, convert distances, choose a formula with matching geometry, establish every direction, and then add vectors. Ampere's law will give us another powerful way to use symmetry in the next class.

quiz.question: A vertical wire carries conventional current upward on the page. Its field to the right is:
quiz.explanation: The right-hand grip rule gives into the page on the right side.

quiz.question: An effectively infinite straight wire carries 5 A. At perpendicular distance 0.05 m, B is approximately:
A finite straight segment has alpha = beta = 45 degrees, I = 5 A and a = 0.05 m, with angles measured from the perpendicular. Its field magnitude is:
A single circular loop has I = 4 A and radius R = 0.1 m. Its center field is:
On that loop's axis at x = R, the ratio B(x)/B0 is:
quiz.explanation: The ratio is R cubed/(R squared + x squared)^(3/2), giving 1/(2 sqrt(2)).

quiz.question: Two long wires 10 cm apart each carry 5 A in opposite directions. At their midpoint, the net field magnitude is:
quiz.explanation: Each contributes 20 microT at 5 cm; opposite current directions make the midpoint fields add.
